title: Seat assignment during checkout
explanation: CheckoutService.checkout finds the best open seat (line 27), then awaits the payment provider (line 32, about 30 ms), and only marks the seat sold afterwards (lines 36-37). While it waits, other checkouts in the same section call first_available and get the same seat, because it still looks open. Each of them is charged and gets an order for that one seat, so seats are double-booked.
expected_fix: Claim the seat before any await: find it and mark it held in one step with nothing that yields in between (or use a lock or a database transaction with a conditional update), then authorize the payment, and release the hold if the payment is declined.
grill_expected_points: The seat is checked for availability before the await on the payment call but only marked sold after it (check-then-act).
Concurrent checkouts in the same section see the same seat as open during that window and all buy it.
Fix it by holding the seat atomically before awaiting payment, and releasing it if the payment fails.
chaos_invariant: Every order has its own seat: orders equal seats sold
grill_question: The attack ran 200 concurrent checkouts and ended up with more orders than seats sold. How can two people end up holding a ticket for the same seat?
grill_follow_up: Between the moment a seat is chosen and the moment it's marked sold, what can another checkout in the same section do?

title: Seat recommendations for groups
explanation: find_adjacent_blocks looks for each seat's right-hand neighbour by scanning the whole list of open seats (line 60), so finding blocks in a 1,000-seat section is O(n^2). It also builds every block before keeping only the first five. It's CPU work inside an async route, so while it runs the event loop can't serve anything else, and under concurrent requests latency climbs for every endpoint.
expected_fix: Index the open seats by (row, number) in a dict or set so each neighbour lookup is O(1), making the search O(n), and stop once enough blocks are found.
grill_expected_points: Each neighbour lookup scans every open seat in the section, so the search is O(n^2).
It runs on the event loop, so concurrent recommendation requests queue up and slow every endpoint.
Index open seats by row and number so each lookup is constant time, and stop after the first few blocks.
chaos_invariant: /sections/{section}/recommendations p95 stays under 1,000 ms at 10 concurrent requests
grill_question: Under concurrent requests, seat recommendations for groups took seconds each. What in that code makes it expensive?
grill_follow_up: For a section with 1,000 seats, roughly how many comparisons does finding one block of four take?
